lesson_title: Two Pumps, One Fist: How Your Heart Beats 100 000 Times a Day
hook_text: Squeeze your fist once a second. That is your heart. Now do it 100 000 times without stopping.
clip_script: Your blood is a delivery fleet. Plasma is the road and the open bakkie, carrying glucose, salts and waste. Red cells are the taxis, millions in a drop, each stuffed with haemoglobin carrying one passenger: oxygen. White cells are security, hunting bacteria. Platelets are the puncture repair kit, plugging cuts. Five litres of fleet, and the engine is your fist. Two pumps side by side. Used blood from the body lands in the right top room, drops to the right bottom room, and is squeezed next door to the lungs. It dumps carbon dioxide, grabs oxygen, turns bright red, never blue, and comes back to the left top room. The left bottom room, with walls three times thicker, fires it down the aorta to your toes. Through the heart twice per lap: double circulation. Highways out, the arteries, thick and stretchy, that throb is your pulse. Footpaths between the cells, capillaries, one cell thick, where oxygen hops off. Back roads home, the veins, with one-way flaps. Keep the pressure around 120 over 80: move, less salt, never smoke.
visual_style: A fist pulses into a two-chambered heart; a stream of red taxis flows right to the lungs, brightens, returns left and bursts down the aorta; roads thin to footpaths between cells and widen again with valve flaps.
pacing: Four quick fleet beats, a steady route through the two pumps, three fast road beats, a one-line health finish.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and recite the full route from vena cava to aorta.
